messages.text: What are the main findings of this paper?

messages.short_answer: The paper reports that non-AI experts explored prompts opportunistically rather than systematically and struggled to make robust, systematic progress. The authors attribute many barriers to human-to-human instruction expectations and a tendency to overgeneralize from few observations. The retrieved passages mainly cover the abstract and introduction, so the detailed study findings below come from PaperLens overview summaries.

sources.text: The paper examines whether non-AI experts can engage in end-user prompt engineering to design LLM-based instructional chatbots, using a prototype design probe that supports developing and systematically evaluating prompting strategies. It motivates the work by noting that LLMs like GPT-3 and ChatGPT enable fluent multi-turn conversation out of the box, while prompt design tools have so far targeted professional programmers and NLP practitioners rather than non-experts. The authors frame prompt engineering as challenging because it requires identifying LLM error contexts, devising strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing their effectiveness. The stated research focus is how non-AI experts intuitively approach prompt design when building instructional chatbots that walk users through activities while answering questions. The abstract reports the central findings, though the pages shown here only introduce them.

These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages of the paper describe end-user prompt design challenges observed in participant interviews with a chatbot persona (CarlaBot) built on a language model. The authors attribute many struggles to two sources: over-generalization from limited experience, and a social lens that applies human-human interaction expectations to the system. Participants struggled to know what behaviors were possible, were confused about their role (coach or director versus the chatbot's persona), and often failed to find effective instructions. The section also notes participants' tendency to mix commands for the bot with instructions meant for users, and ties these behaviors to prior end-user programming and interactive machine learning literature.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

messages.short_answer: I can't write your rationale for you, but I can help you build its structure from what this paper supports. The paper gives you evidence that non-experts explore prompts opportunistically and over-generalise, and it lists limits you would need to address in your own design.

The argument and the final wording should come from your own reasoning about your research.

sources.text: The paper examines whether non-AI experts can engage in end-user prompt engineering to design LLM-based instructional chatbots, using a prototype design probe that supports developing and systematically evaluating prompting strategies. It motivates the work by noting that LLMs like GPT-3 and ChatGPT enable fluent multi-turn conversation out of the box, while prompt design tools have so far targeted professional programmers and NLP practitioners rather than non-experts. The authors frame prompt engineering as challenging because it requires identifying LLM error contexts, devising strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing their effectiveness. The stated research focus is how non-AI experts intuitively approach prompt design when building instructional chatbots that walk users through activities while answering questions. The abstract reports the central findings, though the pages shown here only introduce them.

These pages from the user study section of 'Why Johnny Can't Prompt' describe how ten non-expert participants iteratively designed prompts for a recipe chatbot (CarlaBot) using the BotDesigner tool, with interviewer advice given during the session and analysis via affinity diagrams and service blueprints. The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages describe a user study of non-expert participants writing prompts for an LLM-based chatbot playing the character Carla. They report participants' misconceptions, such as expecting the bot to remember past conversations or be unaffected by a hard reset, and their social, polite phrasing of instructions (e.g., starting with "please"). The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.

These pages discuss a user study of prompt design with a chatbot tool called BotDesigner, focusing on how participants used error labeling and systematic testing. Participants largely stopped labeling errors once they realized the labels were not used by the system, and none used the systematic prompt testing interface, instead declaring victory after a single successful change. The authors describe this as premature victory declaration, similar to overconfident end-user programmers, and note that some professional programmers were more concerned about generalizability. The pages also cover participants struggling to explain why prompts worked or failed across contexts, and a finding that participants favored 'do not' phrasing over the more effective 'do' phrasing, with the authors linking this to early childhood education literature.

These pages discuss a study of how end-users prompt LLM-based chatbots (GPT-3), focusing on mismatches between users' expectations and LLM behavior. Participants were surprised that trivial prompt changes, such as rephrasing or adding a negated 'Don't' instruction, could produce dramatically different outputs, and that plain behavioral descriptions were not always followed. The authors note that participants could rarely explain why the model behaved as it did, given the black-box nature of LLMs. The discussion then offers implications for training and education, including encouraging users to collect more data and perform systematic testing, and suggests searchable example repositories and explanations of instruction time horizons. The pages end by raising design opportunities, such as heuristics for how much data or how many conversations are needed for robustness testing.

These pages of the paper describe end-user prompt design challenges observed in participant interviews with a chatbot persona (CarlaBot) built on a language model. The authors attribute many struggles to two sources: over-generalization from limited experience, and a social lens that applies human-human interaction expectations to the system. Participants struggled to know what behaviors were possible, were confused about their role (coach or director versus the chatbot's persona), and often failed to find effective instructions. The section also notes participants' tendency to mix commands for the bot with instructions meant for users, and ties these behaviors to prior end-user programming and interactive machine learning literature.

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

The authors report that participants took an ad hoc, opportunistic approach, starting from observed chatbot errors such as humorlessness, overly complicated statements, skipping steps, and undesired explanations, then editing the preamble instructions, often by pattern matching existing text. Participants usually declared success after a single successful instance and relied on local testing rather than systematic testing, with limited use of error labeling. The main findings attribute struggles to over-generalization from single observations and to mental models of the system rooted in human-human interaction; the authors note as a limitation that interviewer advice was not uniform across participants.

These pages discuss design implications and limitations from a study of end-user prompt design for LLM-backed chatbots (BotDesigner). They argue that users need more examples of an error class before feeling confident it is resolved, and that tools should make successful examples discoverable and support exploring cause-and-effect between prompt changes and conversational changes. The authors suggest designs that hide the instruction-like nature of prompting or have the app perform socially violating work itself, and note that seamful design may make the app's non-human nature visible. Stated limitations include a small, academic early-adopter sample, limited time for prompt design, and the need for future work on other populations, non-chatbot domains, and the role of social expectations (CASA).

These pages describe the participant table and the interview protocol for a study where participants used the BotDesigner tool to improve a baseline chatbot so it could mimic a conversational style seen in a cooking video. Participants (ten people with varied professions and LLM knowledge) were shown an episode of Back to Back Chef and a transcript with color-coded highlights of humor, analogies, concept simplification, and step confirmation. They had up to one hour to prompt the bot toward these behaviors, with the researchers observing approach rather than final quality, and offering prompt suggestions only after participants got stuck for several minutes. Researchers also reminded participants of labeling, systematic error testing, and edit/replay functions when relevant. Figure 3 shows the opening turns of the expert-amateur cooking transcript used as the target.

The pages also cover participants' bias toward direct instruction over examples, reluctance to copy transcript dialog despite observed gains, and difficulty finding and applying web help. Finally, they note that participants struggled much more with evaluating prompt robustness than with generating prompts, and collected data opportunistically rather than systematically.
